analysis.one_liner: Repeals the 1935 law restricting utility holding companies and replaces it with lighter records-based oversight.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: referred to a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee on April 16, 2001, it received no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935 required utility holding companies — corporate parents that own electric and gas utilities — to register with the Securities and Exchange Commission and submit to structural oversight designed to stop them from shifting costs between regulated utilities and unregulated affiliates. This bill repeals that law and replaces it with a narrower system: federal and state regulators could demand records relevant to rates, and FERC could exempt companies it deemed irrelevant. Utility holding companies would gain freedom from SEC oversight; ratepayer protection would rest almost entirely on after-the-fact records access. The bill never got beyond a subcommittee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Utility holding companies and their unregulated affiliates. Repealing the 1935 act ends SEC registration, approval of mergers and acquisitions by holding companies, and the structural limits on what a utility's corporate parent can do. The replacement regime requires regulators to justify records requests by relevance to rates and lets FERC exempt whole classes of companies and transactions, so oversight becomes reactive and discretionary.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Electric and gas utility holding companies

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935, ending SEC registration and structural regulation of utility holding companies, effective 12 months after enactment.

Replaces it with a regime limited to records access: FERC and state commissions may obtain books and records of holding company affiliates only where relevant to jurisdictional rates, and FERC must exempt qualifying facilities, exempt wholesale generators, and foreign utility companies, and must exempt any person or transaction it finds not relevant to rates.
Retains FERC and state authority to decide whether a utility may recover affiliate-transaction costs in rates, and gives FERC Federal Power Act enforcement powers.

analysis.who_pays: Ratepayers, if regulators fail to detect cost-shifting. The 1935 act's premise was that multi-tier holding companies can bury affiliate costs and asset transfers inside complex corporate structures; the replacement lets regulators look only at records relevant to rates, in many cases only after a state commission has opened a proceeding and identified the records in detail.

drawbacks.text: Repeal removes the SEC's ongoing structural oversight of holding companies, leaving ratepayer protection dependent on records access that is limited to rate-relevant material and can be waived by FERC exemption rules for broad classes of companies and transactions.

State commissions' access requires a written request, records identified in reasonable detail in an existing proceeding, and a relevance showing — a weaker position than the standing examination rights the 1935 act provided, so cost-shifting between a utility and its affiliates could surface late or not at all.

Supporters' honest counterargument: the 1935 act was built for the utility empires of the Depression era and its registration-and-approval regime burdened companies competing in restructured energy markets without clearly protecting rates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a one-sided trade: it delivers immediate deregulatory relief to utility holding companies while converting a standing regulatory regime into a discretionary, after-the-fact records-access system. Consumer protection survives only on paper if regulators lack the practical ability or inclination to invoke it; the exemption authority in Section 7 could hollow out even the records requirement. The bill's stated findings concede the need for 'continued rate protection,' but the mechanism it leaves in place is weaker than the one it repeals.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 2001 and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which passed it down to its Energy and Air Quality subcommittee a month later; nothing further happened, and it died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Chip Pickering introduced the bill on March 20, 2001 with 16 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On April 16, 2001 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, where the record ends — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action is recorded.
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and bills not reported from committee die at the end of a Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electric and gas ratepayers kept the 1935 act's protections for another two years, and the SEC kept jurisdiction over holding companies. Utility holding companies continued operating under a regime they had sought to replace.

industries.industry: Electric and gas utility holding companies
industries.note: Repeal of the 1935 act frees holding companies from SEC registration, merger approval, and structural limits, giving them flexibility to move money between regulated utilities and unregulated affiliates. That flexibility is exactly what ratepayer protection was designed to police, since affiliate costs can flow into utility rates.

Ratepayers keep nominal protections — records access and affiliate-cost review — but lose the standing SEC oversight layer, so they bear the risk if regulators miss cost-shifting. Consumers who see no rate problem gain nothing; consumers exposed to affiliate cost-shifting lose the strongest tool against it.
The bill transfers PUHCA functions and records from the SEC to FERC, ending the SEC's role in utility holding company oversight.
FERC inherits the records-access regime, exemption authority, and Federal Power Act enforcement powers, gaining a new mandate — though a narrower one than the SEC's old brief.
